In many Western countries Friday the 13th is thought unlucky; the fear of it has a name (paraskevidekatriaphobia).

In some countries buildings have no 13th floor and hotels no room 13; the belief is linked to the Last Supper, where there were thirteen at the table, and to the old Norse tale of Loki as the thirteenth guest.
In Chinese, Japanese and Korean the word for four sounds like the word for death, so hospitals and buildings may avoid it.
Eight sounds like the word for prosperity in Chinese, so phone numbers, car plates and addresses with 8 are prized; the Beijing Olympics opened on 8/8/08 at 8 pm.
Seven is lucky in many Western cultures, perhaps from the seven days of Creation and the seven heavens in several religions.
In Italy and some Spanish-speaking countries the unlucky day is Tuesday the 13th or Friday the 17th, as the Roman numeral XVII can be rearranged as VIXI, "I have lived", meaning death.
The number of the beast in the Book of Revelation, avoided by some as an address or a car plate.
Nine sounds like the word for "long-lasting", and is the number of the emperor.
In the United States and much of Europe a black cat crossing your path is bad luck, a belief linked to medieval ideas of witches; in Britain and Japan black cats are lucky.
A British rhyme, "one for sorrow, two for joy", says that seeing a single magpie is a sign of sorrow; people often greet it to avoid the bad luck.
In many Western cultures, a symbol of wisdom; in parts of India, Africa and the Middle East a hooting owl is thought to be a sign of death or bad news, while in other places the owl is lucky.
In Europe the raven was linked to death and war. In India, crows are linked with ancestors, and a crow cawing is said to mean a guest is coming.
Carried for luck in the United States and Europe, a belief which is said to come from the idea that rabbits, which live underground, were linked with magic.
In India, China, Japan and other places, whistling at night is said to call snakes or ghosts.
Fishermen and sailors in several countries consider bananas aboard a ship bad luck, a belief that is said to come from old ships carrying bananas that spoiled fast and brought spiders.
In Europe a ladybird landing on you is a sign of good luck.

The belief that a harmful look, especially of envy, can bring harm is found from Greece and Turkey to the Middle East, South Asia and Latin America. Charms such as the blue glass eye in Turkey, the hamsa hand in the Middle East, or lemons and chillies hung at the door in India are used to protect.
A horseshoe hung above the door, points up, is lucky in many Western countries, said to catch the luck, and to have protected against witches and the devil as iron was thought to repel evil.
The rare four-leaf clover is considered lucky, in particular in Ireland, where clovers are a national symbol.
People tap wood after saying something hopeful to avoid tempting fate; a belief said to come from old ideas about spirits living in trees.
A gesture for luck in many countries, thought to come from the early Christian sign of the cross.
In many countries, a shooting star is an occasion to make a wish and keep it a secret.
Two people pull on the wishbone of a chicken or turkey; the one with the larger piece gets a wish, a custom from Europe and the United States.
In many countries a coin thrown into a fountain or well brings luck or a wish, a custom that goes back to ancient offerings to water spirits.
Breaking a mirror is said to bring seven years of bad luck, a belief traced to the Romans, who thought that a mirror held part of the soul and that the soul renewed itself in seven years.

Thought unlucky in much of the West; one explanation is that a ladder against a wall makes a triangle, an old symbol of the Trinity, and walking through it breaks it. The practical reason is that something may fall on you.
Spilling salt is said to bring a quarrel, and throwing a pinch over the left shoulder is said to undo the harm. Salt was precious in the past.
Said to bring bad luck in Britain and the United States; the practical reason is that it can break things or poke an eye.
A clock as a gift in China
Giving a clock is avoided in Chinese culture, because the phrase for giving a clock sounds like the phrase for attending a funeral.
Elders in India, Korea and elsewhere advise against it. Before electric light it was dangerous to cut nails in the dark.
In Japan, China and Korea, chopsticks standing in a bowl of rice look like incense sticks at a funeral, so it is considered very rude.
In many cultures, an itching palm means money coming or going; the hand varies. See also our shakun pages.
Seeing the bride before the wedding

In Western weddings it is said to be unlucky for the groom to see the bride in her dress before the ceremony; the custom comes from arranged marriages in which the couple should not meet before the wedding.
A bride in England and the United States should wear or carry something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue, a rhyme from the nineteenth century.
Throwing rice or petals over a newly married couple is a sign of wishes for fertility and plenty, in many cultures.
Not buying baby things before the birth
In several cultures, including India, Jewish and Chinese families, it is considered bad luck to prepare for a baby before it is born, so as not to tempt fate.
Red is the colour of luck and joy in China and India, so brides wear red, and children and gifts are decorated with red.
In India and China white is the colour of mourning; in the West it is black.
Covering mirrors in a house of mourning
In Jewish and some other traditions, mirrors are covered when someone has died.
Holding your breath at a graveyard
A child's game in many countries, said to prevent the spirits from entering you.
